caption:
A radar image is not a photograph. It is a measurement of how a surface scatters a radio pulse back to the sensor — surface roughness, moisture, angle. Water looks smooth and returns almost nothing. Flooded fields look like open water. Wet pavement can look like a river. None of that is visible light. It has to be read, not just looked at.

This is why radar interpretation takes trained analysts, not a glance. Two returns that look identical on a screen can mean standing floodwater or a smooth road surface after rain. Get the read wrong and the flag is worse than useless — it sends a patrol or a warning to the wrong place.

The payoff is real: radar sees through cloud cover, day or night, when optical sensors are blind. But the tradeoff is that every pass demands correct interpretation, not just a bigger image. Resolution without a trained read is just a sharper wrong answer.
